1.title: Projects: Instructions and Knowledge
1.text: Welcome to Module eleven: Projects: Instructions and Knowledge. This module covers projects: instructions and knowledge. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. What a Project is and what it contains. How to write effective project instructions (system-level instructions). How to choose and organize knowledge. How R A G extends a Project's capacity. How Projects differ from account instructions, memory and Skills.

1.title: Case Check-In: Cedarbrook's Customer-Care Project
1.text: Our running case is Cedarbrook Outfitters. Cedarbrook's Customer-Care Project. Customer care creates a Project named "Care Replies". Its instructions set the brand voice, the escalation rules and the refund policy summary. Its knowledge holds the returns policy, product F A Q s and approved reply examples. Every agent who opens a chat in the Project gets the same background, with no pasting.

1.title: What a Project Is
1.text: What a Project Is. A Project is a self-contained workspace with its own chat history, instructions and knowledge base. Everything in it is available to every chat inside it.

1.title: What a Project Is, continued
1.text: What a Project Is, continued. The figure shows this: A Project holds instructions, knowledge and its own memory, and every chat inside it uses them.

1.title: What a Project Is, continued
1.text: What a Project Is, continued. Project instructions. What it is: Standing guidance applied to all chats in the Project. Typical content: Role, audience, tone, format, rules, how to handle uncertainty. Knowledge. What it is: Uploaded files and text Claude can use as background. Typical content: Policies, F A Q s, product sheets, style guides, templates, examples. Chats. What it is: Conversations that inherit the above. Typical content: Daily tasks. Project memory. What it is: Memory kept for this Project only. Typical content: Learned preferences of this work. Projects are available to all users, including free accounts, with a limit of five Projects on free plans.

1.title: What a Project Is, continued
1.text: What a Project Is, continued. Why use a Project: consistency, no re-pasting, shared context for a team, and less usage because project content is cached and reused. Team and Enterprise: Projects can be shared with specific people or the organization. Can view equals see contents and chat but not edit; Can edit equals change instructions and knowledge and manage members. Owners can turn sharing off. Exam tip: If the same background is needed again and again, the answer is a Project (instructions plus knowledge), not longer prompts.

1.title: Writing Effective Instructions
1.text: Writing Effective Instructions. Project instructions work like a briefing for a new colleague who starts every chat with no memory. They are the "system-level" layer: they apply before your message.

1.title: Writing Effective Instructions, continued
1.text: Writing Effective Instructions, continued. The figure shows this: A strong instruction set names the role, audience, goals, tone, format, rules, how to handle uncertainty, when to escalate, and gives examples.

1.title: Writing Effective Instructions, continued
1.text: Writing Effective Instructions, continued. Role and purpose. What to write: Who Claude is here and for what. Example: "You help Cedarbrook customer-care agents draft replies to customers". Audience. What to write: Who reads the output. Example: "Customers aged twenty-five to sixty-five, non-technical". Tone and style. What to write: Voice with a short example. Example: "Warm, direct, no jargon; see example replies in knowledge". Format. What to write: Structure and length. Example: "Under one hundred twenty words; greeting, answer, next step". Rules. What to write: Must and must not. Example: "Never promise refunds over two hundred dollars; never share other customers' data". Source of truth. What to write: Where facts come from. Example: "Use the returns policy file; if it is silent, say so".

1.title: Writing Effective Instructions, continued
1.text: Writing Effective Instructions, continued. Uncertainty. What to write: What to do when unsure. Example: "Say you are not sure and recommend a supervisor". Escalation. What to write: When to hand over. Example: "Complaints about safety go to a manager immediately". Examples. What to write: One or two good outputs. Example: "See the three approved replies in knowledge". Good practice. Be specific and explain why ("Keep replies short because agents read them on a phone"). Use clear sections or bullet points, not one long paragraph. Keep instructions short and focused: long instructions use up context; put task-specific instructions in the chat instead. State what Claude should do when information is missing.

1.title: Writing Effective Instructions, continued
1.text: Writing Effective Instructions, continued. Test with real examples, including awkward ones; revise after seeing results. Version and date the instructions and name an owner (Module twelve). Do not place sensitive data, passwords or personal details in instructions or knowledge unless policy allows it (Module thirteen). Exam tip: Strong instructions state role, audience, format, rules, source of truth, uncertainty behavior and escalation. A one-line "be helpful" is a weak answer.

1.title: Choosing and Organizing Knowledge
1.text: Choosing and Organizing Knowledge. Upload what Claude needs repeatedly: policies, F A Q s, product sheets, style guides, templates, examples of good outputs. Quality over quantity. Out-of-date, duplicated or contradictory files confuse answers. Remove files you no longer need. Use clear, descriptive filenames (for example, Returns-Policy-current.pdf) and group related documents in the same Project. Reference documents by name in your questions: "According to the Returns Policy,...". Limits: project files are limited to about thirty megabytes each, with text extracted (except for P D F s that include visuals). Total content must fit the context window unless R A G is on.

1.title: Choosing and Organizing Knowledge, continued
1.text: Choosing and Organizing Knowledge, continued. Google Docs from Drive can be added to a Project and stay in sync (private Projects) (Module twelve). Files in the Project are cached; reuse costs less usage. Caches expire after inactivity. Retrieval augmented generation (R A G).

1.title: Choosing and Organizing Knowledge, continued
1.text: Choosing and Organizing Knowledge, continued. What it does. When knowledge nears the context limit, Claude retrieves only the relevant parts with a project knowledge search tool instead of loading everything. Capacity. Up to about ten times more content. Availability. Paid plans; automatic; shown by an indicator. Control. You cannot switch it manually; Claude uses in-context processing when possible. Quality. Designed to keep response quality and speed. Best practices. Upload relevant content upfront, clear filenames, related documents together, reference documents by name.

1.title: Projects Compared with Other Context Tools
1.text: Projects Compared with Other Context Tools. The figure shows this: Account instructions apply everywhere, Project instructions only inside the Project, memory learns from chats, and Skills load only when a task needs them.

1.title: Projects Compared with Other Context Tools, continued
1.text: Projects Compared with Other Context Tools, continued. Instructions for Claude (account). Scope: All your chats. Best for: Personal preferences: your role, tone, formats. Project instructions and knowledge. Scope: Chats inside that Project. Best for: A body of work with shared background. Memory. Scope: Learned across chats (separate per Project). Best for: Continuity; not for must-have rules. Skills. Scope: Loaded only when relevant. Best for: A repeatable method or format (Module twelve). Styles. Scope: The tone and format of replies. Best for: Writing style. Exam tip: Put standing context in the Project and keep the instructions short and specific; move one-off details into the chat.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Project: Workspace with instructions, knowledge, chats and its own memory. Free plan: Up to five Projects. Instructions: Role, audience, tone, format, rules, source of truth, uncertainty, escalation, examples. Style of instructions: Specific, explain why, sectioned, short; test and revise. Knowledge: Current, clean, clearly named, grouped; remove stale files; about thirty megabytes per file. R A G: Automatic on paid plans near the limit; up to about ten times; retrieves relevant parts. Sharing: Team and Enterprise: Can view versus Can edit. Do not store: Sensitive personal data or secrets unless policy allows. Compare: Account instructions (all chats), Project (inside), memory (learned), Skills (when relevant).

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. Customer care agents paste the same policy summary into every chat. What is the best fix? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. A Project provides standing instructions and knowledge to every chat.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. Which Project instruction is most effective? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. It states role, tone, format, source of truth and uncertainty behavior.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. A Project contains an outdated two thousand twenty-three policy next to the current one, and answers sometimes contradict each other. What should the owner do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Out-of-date or conflicting knowledge produces inconsistent answers, so the owner should keep only the current, clearly named version.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. A Project's knowledge is large and nears the context limit. On a paid plan, what happens? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Retrieval augmented generation turns on automatically on paid plans and retrieves only the relevant parts, extending capacity by about ten times.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. Which statement about project instructions versus account instructions is correct? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Account instructions apply to all your chats, while project instructions apply only inside that Project, so scope is the difference.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. Select two. Which two should not be stored in Project instructions or knowledge without approval? The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and E. Personal data and secrets do not belong there unless policy explicitly allows it.

1.title: Practice Question 7
1.text: Question seven. A teammate with "Can view" access to a shared Project tries to change the instructions. What happens? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Can view lets people read and chat, not edit.

1.title: Practice Question 8
1.text: Question eight. Why keep Project instructions short and move task-specific details into the chat? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Concise, focused instructions save context and usage, while task-specific details can be given in the chat where they are needed.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all eight answers. Question one: A. Question two: A. Question three: D. Question four: B. Question five: D. Question six: B and E. Question seven: A. Question eight: D. In the next module, we continue the course.
